name: DoS attack construction and countermeasure/responsibility analysis
theory_paragraphs: Start from the big picture. Security people summarize the goals of protection with the \term{CIA triad}: \term{confidentiality} (only authorized parties can read data), \term{integrity} (only authorized parties can change data), and \term{availability} (authorized parties can actually \emph{use} the system when they need to). A \term{denial-of-service (DoS) attack} is any attack on the third property: it does not steal or modify data, it makes a service slow, unreachable, or crashed so that legitimate users cannot use it. When the attack is launched simultaneously from many machines (usually a \term{botnet} of hacked devices controlled by the attacker), it is called a \term{distributed DoS (DDoS)}. \imp{A DoS attack works by exhausting some limited resource.} The whole analysis of any DoS question is: find \emph{which resource} runs out, and \emph{who} can stop that from happening.

Which resource can be exhausted? Four recurring targets: \begin{tightitem}\item \term{Bandwidth}: the attacker's traffic (or traffic it causes) fills the victim's network link, so legitimate packets are dropped or delayed. Example: an \term{ICMP flood} (huge numbers of ping packets).\item \term{State / memory}: the server keeps a table entry per client or per pending connection; the attacker creates so many entries that the table is full. Example: the \term{SYN flood}.\item \term{Computation}: one cheap request forces expensive server work (verifying a signature, scanning a file, generating megabytes of output), so the CPU saturates.\item \term{Correctness}: a single malformed input crashes the program (buffer overflow, unhandled exception). \end{tightitem} The key economic insight: the attacker wins when \imp{the attacker spends less than the victim loses}. If one small packet forces the victim to spend a lot of bandwidth, memory, or CPU, even an attacker with a slow home connection can kill a big server.

To understand the classic attacks you must know one networking fact: \term{source IP addresses can be forged on connectionless protocols}. UDP and ICMP are \term{connectionless}: a machine just emits a packet with a claimed ``from'' address and nobody checks it. So the attacker Mallory can send a UDP packet whose source address is the \emph{victim's} address --- this is called \term{IP spoofing}. TCP is different: before any data flows, TCP runs a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). The machine claiming an address must actually receive the SYN-ACK sent back to that address, which a spoofer cannot do, so \imp{TCP verifies the source address, UDP and ICMP do not}. A second attacker capability to keep in mind is the \term{man in the middle (MITM)}: an attacker positioned on the network path between two parties, who can read, modify and retransmit the messages passing through.

Spoofing enables the two most famous amplification attacks. \term{Reflection}: Mallory sends many small requests, each with the \emph{victim's} spoofed source address, to many innocent servers; each server politely sends its reply to the victim. The victim is flooded by traffic from servers it never contacted, and Mallory's own address never appears. \term{Amplification}: the reply is much bigger than the request, so the flood is bigger than anything Mallory could send herself --- a classic example is a $\approx 60$-byte DNS query producing a $\approx 4$~KB answer (about $60\times$). \imp{The reflector supplies the bandwidth, so the attacker's own bandwidth is irrelevant.} This is exactly why exam questions say ``assume the attacker has less bandwidth than the victim'' --- they want you to realize that this does not save the victim.

The \term{SYN flood} targets state instead of bandwidth. When a server receives a TCP SYN it allocates a \emph{half-open} entry in its \term{connection table} and waits for the final ACK. If Mallory sends a stream of SYNs with spoofed, non-existent sources, the ACKs never arrive; the table fills with half-open entries until \imp{legitimate new connections can no longer be accepted}. Each cheap SYN costs the server a table slot until a timeout expires, so again a weak attacker defeats a strong server. Standard fixes: shorter timeouts on half-open entries, per-source-IP limits, and \term{SYN cookies} (encode the connection state inside the TCP sequence number so the server stores \emph{nothing} until the client proves it is real by returning the cookie in its ACK).

Countermeasures and --- crucially for the exam --- \emph{who deploys them}. \begin{tightitem}\item \term{Ingress/egress filtering (BCP 38)}: routers drop packets whose source address is impossible for the network they came from. This kills spoofing, but it must be deployed \emph{at the source}, i.e. by \term{the attacker's ISP}. \imp{Filtering at the victim cannot work: by the time the packets reach the victim, its upstream link is already full.}\item At the service: authenticate the \emph{whole} message --- with a \term{message authentication code (MAC)}, a short keyed tag that only someone holding the shared secret key can produce, or with a digital signature over every field --- and include a \term{nonce} (a fresh random value) or timestamp against \term{replay} (an attacker re-sending an old, valid message to trigger its effect again), verify the source \emph{before} committing memory or CPU (TCP handshake, challenge-response cookie), rate-limit, and add \term{redundancy} (the application runs on several servers behind different gateways, ideally in different geographic areas, so no single link congestion kills it).\item Responsibility: the ISP deploys filtering; the service fixes its own authentication and resource logic; \imp{neither the victim nor its cloud provider can filter a flood they receive}, because they are not the network provider carrying the attack traffic.\end{tightitem}
theory_cheatsheet: DoS = attack on \term{availability}: exhaust bandwidth, state, computation, or correctness.
Economics: attacker wins when one cheap request costs the victim a lot (bandwidth, memory, CPU).
UDP/ICMP source IPs are forgeable (connectionless); the TCP handshake verifies the source.
\term{Reflection} $+$ \term{amplification}: spoof the victim's IP, let big servers flood it (DNS: $\approx 60$~B request $\rightarrow$ $\approx 4$~KB reply).
\term{SYN flood} fills the half-open connection table; fix with SYN cookies, timeouts, per-IP caps.
\imp{Ingress filtering (BCP 38) belongs to the attacker's ISP} --- victim-side filtering fails because the upstream link is already congested; redundancy across gateways is the service-side answer.
identify_givens: A request--response or publish--subscribe service/protocol described message by message, usually over UDP with spoofable source IP addresses and weak or missing source authentication (no MAC/signature over the whole message, or a check covering only part of the message). An attacker model is stated: the attacker has less bandwidth than the victim, may eavesdrop or intercept traffic, but cannot recover keys. Sometimes a named flood (SYN/ICMP) or a service whose work-per-request is expensive or whose replies are much larger than the requests.
identify_target: Describe concretely how the attacker performs a DoS against a stated victim (the server itself or a third-party client) despite having less bandwidth; then describe how the vulnerability can be countered and, when asked, who must deploy the countermeasure (the attacker's ISP, the service, or the cloud provider).
identify_keywords: describe how this vulnerability can be countered
strategy_name: Exploit spoofing + asymmetry (amplification or state exhaustion), then authenticate the source

algorithm.detail: List each protocol message with its transport and effect:\begin{tightitem}\item transport: UDP/ICMP $\rightarrow$ \term{source IP is forgeable}; TCP $\rightarrow$ handshake-verified source;\item effect: what work or traffic each message triggers at the server (replies, stored state per client, downstream messages to third parties).\end{tightitem}Beginner tip: write this as a small table (message, transport, cost) before judging anything.

Check what actually proves the sender's identity. An unauthenticated UDP source field can simply be forged. A subtler gap: only \emph{part} of the message is protected (e.g. only $X = E(IP_i, K_i)$ is verified while $L$ travels in plaintext), so a man in the middle tampers with the unprotected fields. Always ask: which bytes lie \emph{inside} the authenticated portion, and which lie outside?

Spot the \term{amplification factor} (one small request triggers many or large replies: $L$ bytes split into 512~KB blocks, or one publish causes one message per subscriber per topic) or the \term{exhaustion target} (server CPU per verification, memory, connection table or thread pool grows per forged request or half-open SYN). The asymmetry is what makes a weak attacker dangerous --- if you cannot find one, re-read the protocol.

Combine the gap and the asymmetry:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{reflection/amplification}: spoof the victim's IP (or raise the unprotected $L$) so the server floods the victim with traffic;\item \term{state/computation exhaustion}: mass-forge requests so the server's own memory, table or CPU saturates.\end{tightitem}State explicitly why \emph{less bandwidth than the victim} does not matter: \imp{the server supplies the bandwidth and the state}.

Authenticate the \emph{whole} message and verify the source before committing resources: use TCP (the handshake proves the source address) or sign/MAC/encrypt everything, e.g. $E(IP_i \,\|\, L, K_i)$ so tampering with $L$ is detected; add a nonce/sequence number/expiration against \term{replay}; commit no memory or computation until the source is proven (challenge-response); add rate limiting.

If asked who deploys what: \begin{tightitem}\item spoofing is fixed at the source by the \term{attacker's ISP} via ingress/egress filtering (BCP 38);\item victim-side or cloud-provider filtering fails because \imp{the upstream link is already congested};\item the service fixes its own authentication, resource-commitment logic, redundancy across gateways, and (for SYN floods) SYN cookies/backlog handling.\end{tightitem}

variations.name: Tampering instead of spoofing
variations.detail: In dasak19 P1 the protocol does authenticate the client ($D(X, K_i) = IP_i$ is checked), so pure IP spoofing fails --- the trap is to overlook that $L$ is sent in \emph{plaintext}: a man in the middle raises $L$ and gets amplification anyway. Adapt Step 2: enumerate which fields lie \emph{inside} the authenticated portion and attack the ones outside.

variations.name: Victim is the server, not a client
variations.detail: In dasak18 P1 the attacker targets the server itself: mass forged subscriptions exhaust server memory, or one forged publish forces the server to emit hundreds of messages. Adapt Step 4: choose between \term{traffic amplification} against third parties and \term{state/resource exhaustion} of the server --- the official solution accepts either.

variations.name: Role reversal: replay to force expensive work
variations.detail: Some sittings replace spoofing with \term{replay}: unauthenticated (or nonce-less signed) messages are re-sent to force repeated expensive server work (malware scans, many hash comparisons). The fix still follows Step 5: nonce/timestamp inside the signed portion plus rate limiting.

variations.name: Named flood with responsibility question
variations.detail: 2022/NEN-style variants name the threat (SYN flood, ICMP flood, amplification via open resolvers) and ask \emph{who must act}. Trap: saying the victim or its cloud provider should filter --- the upstream link is already saturated, so ingress filtering (BCP 38) belongs to the attacker's ISP; SYN floods additionally need cookies/backlog fixes at the server.

walkthrough_problem: Denial of service. To save battery, a fleet of constrained parking sensors offloads cryptographic work to a verification oracle O run by the city. The protocol is as follows (all messages sent over UDP): To request a check, sensor $S_i$ sends $\langle IP_i, IP_O, C, M, \sigma \rangle$ to O, where $C$ is the claimed signer's certificate, $M$ a firmware manifest, and $\sigma$ the signature to verify. O performs a full certificate-chain validation and signature verification (about 40~ms of CPU per request), then sends a \emph{verification report} back to $IP_i$: a 4~KB document containing the parsed certificate chain, every intermediate \term{certificate revocation list (CRL)} entry consulted (a CRL is a published list of cancelled certificates that must be checked during chain validation), and the verdict. Describe how a malicious user can abuse this service to mount a denial-of-service attack, given that the attacker has less bandwidth than the victim, and describe how the vulnerability can be countered.

walkthrough_steps.work: One \emph{verify-request} (sensor $\rightarrow$ O) triggers two costly effects: (a) expensive CPU work at O --- certificate-chain validation plus signature verification, $\approx 40$~ms per request --- and (b) a 4~KB report sent back to the claimed source address. Everything is UDP. \emph{Why this step:} you cannot attack what you have not mapped; listing ``what does one message cost the server, and where does output go'' exposes both candidate resources (CPU and outbound bandwidth). \emph{Mistake to avoid:} do not jump straight to ``spoofing'' before noting the costs --- the costs are what make the attack work.

The request carries no credential, MAC or proof of source. O trusts the claimed $IP_i$ field of a UDP datagram and starts computing (and replying) \emph{before} any source verification. Because UDP is connectionless, $IP_i$ can be forged: the attacker simply writes any address she likes into the packet. \emph{Why this matters:} an attack needs both an asymmetry (Step 3) and a way to aim it; the missing authentication is what lets the attacker aim O's output at someone else.

There are two asymmetries: (a) \emph{traffic amplification}: one small request (a certificate, a manifest and a signature --- at most a few hundred bytes) makes O emit a 4~KB report, many times larger, to an address of the attacker's choosing; (b) \emph{computational exhaustion}: each cheap request burns $\approx 40$~ms of O's CPU. \emph{Why beginners miss this:} they look only for ``big reply vs small request''; the exam rewards noticing \emph{both} kinds of cost asymmetry, so always check CPU/memory as well as bytes.

Attack on a victim host: Mallory sends a stream of verify-requests with the \emph{victim's} IP as source; O reflects a 4~KB report per request and floods the victim's link --- Mallory's small uplink suffices because O supplies the bandwidth (reflection $+$ amplification). Simultaneously, attack on O itself: the forged requests keep O's CPUs at 100\% on chain validation, so \emph{legitimate sensors} wait indefinitely --- a denial of service with far less bandwidth than O's own link capacity. \emph{Key sentence to write on the exam:} the phrase ``less bandwidth than the victim'' is neutralized because \imp{the server supplies the bandwidth and the state}.

Commit no work before the source is proven: switch to TCP (the handshake verifies the source address) or use a \term{challenge-response cookie} --- O first replies with a cheap nonce and only starts validation when the requester returns it, which a spoofer cannot do because she never receives packets sent to the spoofed address. Authenticate the \emph{whole} request with a MAC/signature over $\langle IP_i, C, M, \sigma, \text{nonce} \rangle$; rate-limit reports per destination IP and cap CPU per request. \emph{Mistake to avoid:} proposing only ``use encryption'' without saying \emph{what} is encrypted --- graders want the whole-message binding.

Spoofing is eliminated at the source by the \emph{attacker's ISP} deploying ingress/egress filtering (BCP 38), dropping packets whose source address does not match its routing tables. Dropping the reflected reports at the victim (or its cloud provider) does not help, because the victim's upstream link is already congested by the time the packets arrive. O itself must fix the commit-work-before-verification design. \emph{Why:} the exam's ``who is in charge'' phrasing is testing exactly this allocation --- ISP fixes spoofing, service fixes its own logic, the victim can do nothing about a saturated link.

exam_questions.problem: Denial of service. A news feed service S allows clients to subscribe to news published by content providers. The protocol: (1) to subscribe to a topic $T$, client $C_i$ sends the UDP message $\langle IP_i, IP_S, T \rangle$ to S, where $IP_i$ is the IP of the client and $IP_S$ the IP of the server; (2) to publish a news item, publisher $P_j$ sends the UDP message $\langle IP_j, IP_S, N, T_1, \dots, T_n \rangle$ to S, where $N$ is the content and $T_1, \dots, T_n$ a list of topics; (3) as soon as a news item is published, the server sends a UDP message $\langle IP_S, IP_i, D \rangle$ to every client registered for at least one of the relevant topics. Describe how this system can be abused by a malicious user in order to perform a DOS of the server S. Assume the attacker has less bandwidth than the victim. Describe how this vulnerability can be countered.

solution_steps.work: Three message types, all UDP (so every source address is forgeable): a \emph{subscribe} makes S \emph{store state} (a registration binding $IP_i$ to topic $T$); a \emph{publish} makes S \emph{emit traffic} (one notification per registered client per matching topic). Note the two candidate resources immediately: S's \emph{memory} (the subscription table) and S's \emph{outbound bandwidth/CPU} (the fan-out of notifications).

Neither message type carries any credential, MAC or signature: S trusts the claimed $IP_i$ / $IP_j$ fields of spoofable UDP datagrams. Anyone can subscribe arbitrary addresses to arbitrary topics and can publish arbitrary news under any publisher's name.

(a) \emph{Fan-out amplification}: one small publish message with $n$ topics forces S to generate and send one notification per subscriber of those topics --- potentially hundreds of messages per single attacker packet. (b) \emph{State exhaustion}: each forged subscribe adds a permanent row to S's registration table, so unbounded memory growth per tiny request.

Official solution: the attacker spoofs the IP of several clients $C_i$ and registers them to hundreds of topics; then spoofs the IP of a publisher $P_j$ and publishes an article tagged with hundreds of topics. This forces the server to send hundreds of notification messages to many clients --- the attacker's handful of packets have multiplied into a flood of server work and traffic, so the attacker's inferior bandwidth is irrelevant (the server supplies both the bandwidth and the state). \emph{Alternatively}, the attacker simply exhausts all of the server's memory by continuing to subscribe (forged) users indefinitely.

Official solution: use TCP or some sort of authentication. Expanded: the TCP handshake verifies that the claimed source address really receives packets, killing blind spoofing; or authenticate every subscribe/publish message (MAC or signature over the whole message, with a nonce or timestamp against replay) so forged registrations and forged publishes are rejected before S stores state or emits traffic.

exam_questions.answer: Spoofed subscribes register many (fake) clients to hundreds of topics and one spoofed publish tagged with hundreds of topics forces S to emit hundreds of messages (or forged subscribes simply exhaust S's memory); counter by using TCP or authenticating the messages.

exam_questions.problem: Denial of service. A random program generator service S allows clients to generate random data. Each client $C_i$ shares a symmetric key $K_i$ with the service. Protocol: (1) to ask for random data, client $C_i$ sends the UDP message $\langle IP_i, IP_S, X, L \rangle$ to S, where $X = E(IP_i, K_i)$ is the encryption of $IP_i$ under $K_i$ and $L$ is the number of bytes requested; (2) the service checks that $D(X, K_i) = IP_i$ and terminates if the check fails; (3) if the check succeeds, the service generates $L$ bytes of random data, splits the result into blocks of 512~KB, and sends each block $D_j$ to the client via UDP messages $\langle IP_S, IP_i, D_j \rangle$. Describe how this system can be abused by an attacker (that is not one of the clients) to perform a DOS of one of the clients $C_i$. Assume the attacker has less bandwidth than the victim and cannot recover the key $K_i$ even by analyzing traffic. Then describe how the vulnerability can be countered.

solution_steps.work: One request in, $L$ bytes of random data out, delivered in 512~KB UDP blocks to the claimed $IP_i$. Transport is UDP both ways. The expensive effect is S's outbound traffic; the destination of that traffic is taken from the message itself.

The source address \emph{is} authenticated: only a holder of $K_i$ can produce $X = E(IP_i, K_i)$ passing the check $D(X, K_i) = IP_i$, and the attacker cannot recover $K_i$, so pure IP spoofing fails. \emph{But} the check covers only $X$: the length field $L$ travels in \emph{plaintext}, outside the encrypted portion. A man in the middle can therefore tamper with $L$ without breaking the check. Beginner trap: seeing ``encryption + check'' and concluding the message is authenticated --- always ask \emph{which fields} are inside the protected part.

Amplification: raising $L$ to a huge value makes S emit $L$ bytes (in 512~KB blocks) for a single small request --- e.g. $L = 1$~GB means about $2000$ blocks from one request. The attacker injects a few bytes; the server floods the client with gigabytes.

Official solution: a man-in-the-middle attack. The attacker intercepts a legitimate request $\langle IP_i, IP_S, X, L \rangle$ from client $C_i$, changes $L$ to a much larger value, and retransmits the message. The check $D(X, K_i) = IP_i$ still passes ($X$ was not touched), so S generates $L$ bytes of random data and streams them in 512~KB blocks to $IP_i$ --- the victim client $C_i$ is flooded with traffic it never asked for, and the attacker's own bandwidth is irrelevant because S supplies the flood.

Official solution: sign/encrypt the \emph{whole} message, i.e. send $E(IP_i \,\|\, L, K_i)$; when the server decrypts it, it checks that the embedded IP matches (which plays the role of a MAC), so any tampering with $L$ is detected. To also avoid replay attacks (re-sending an old valid request), each message should carry a sequence number or an expiration time.

exam_questions.answer: A man in the middle intercepts a request, enlarges the plaintext field $L$, and retransmits it, making S flood client $C_i$ with up to $L$ bytes; fix by encrypting/signing the whole message, $E(IP_i \,\|\, L, K_i)$, plus a sequence number or expiration time against replay.

exam_questions.problem: Denial of Service. Context: NEN (``Never-Ending Notes'') is a company whose service keeps users' notes and synchronizes them across devices; you are hired to do the security of the NEN product. Threat: the server running the NEN service could be targeted by an ICMP flood attack. Mitigation: NEN have no proposals and ask you. Assignment: which countermeasure can be used to prevent or mitigate this attack, and who is in charge of it?

solution_steps.step_ref: Steps 1+3 (map the flow; identify the exhaustion target)
solution_steps.work: The attack is already named, so Steps 2 and 4 (finding an authentication gap and constructing the attack) are not needed --- what remains is to classify the asymmetry. An ICMP flood is a pure \emph{bandwidth} exhaustion attack: a (possibly distributed) mass of ping packets saturates the link leading to NEN's server. Note what is \emph{not} the issue here: there is no protocol-level flaw in the NEN application to patch --- the resource being exhausted is the network link itself.

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 6 (responsibility analysis: why the victim cannot fix it)
solution_steps.work: Dropping the malicious packets at NEN's server or at NEN's cloud provider cannot help: by the time the packets arrive there, NEN's \emph{upstream link is already congested} --- the damage (a full link) is done upstream of any point NEN controls. Beginner trap: proposing a bigger firewall at the victim; a firewall can only drop packets that have \emph{already consumed} the victim's bandwidth.

solution_steps.step_ref: Steps 5+6 (countermeasure at the source, and who deploys it)
solution_steps.work: Official solution: the most obvious countermeasure is \term{ingress filtering} close to the attacker, preventing the attacker from spoofing IP addresses and enabling the congested routers to identify and drop malicious traffic. Neither NEN nor its cloud provider can deploy this, since they are not the network service providers: \imp{the ISP of the attacker is in charge of deploying the countermeasure} (this is the BCP 38 idea: drop packets whose source address is inconsistent with the network they originate from).

Official solution, alternative: NEN could design the server application to run on multiple servers, and the cloud provider could deploy it on machines connected via \emph{different gateways}, ideally in several geographic areas. It is then hard for an attacker to congest the links of several routers at once, so the service stays available even while one site is flooded. Responsibility split: the attacker-side filtering belongs to the attacker's ISP; the redundancy deployment is shared between NEN (application design) and its cloud provider (multi-gateway hosting).

exam_questions.answer: Deploy ingress filtering close to the attacker (in charge: the attacker's ISP --- neither NEN nor its cloud provider can, since they are not network providers); alternatively, run the service redundantly on servers behind different gateways/geographic areas via the cloud provider.
